Title: September 10, 2026 City of Boulder City Council Study Session - 2027 Recommended Budget

Topic1.Title: Opening remarks and 2027 budget overview by City Manager and CFO
Topic1.Summary: City Manager Nuria Rivera-Vandermark introduced the 2027 recommended budget, noting hard trade-offs and reductions after several years of constrained revenue. CFO Christa Morrison presented the total of $552.6 million across all funds, a $135.4 million capital budget, and a 2.3% operating increase, the second slowest since the pandemic. She described sales tax dependence, inflation pressures, and personnel costs making up 41% of operating spending.

Topic2.Title: Budget officer presentation on revenues, assumptions and community engagement
Topic2.Summary: Budget Officer Charlotte Husky outlined budget assumptions including a $6.3 million general fund gap and reductions made in response. Revenue changes include a transportation maintenance fee, a recreational marijuana sales tax increase from 3.5% to 5.5%, and utility fee increases. The Fund Our Future community conversations with over 500 residents informed priorities such as wildfire, facilities maintenance, public safety, and affordable housing.

Topic3.Title: Operating budget changes by goal area
Topic3.Summary: Scott Carpenter, principal budget analyst, highlighted operating changes across the sustainability, equity, and resilience goals. Items included a $4.3 million increase for city facilities maintenance, $11 million in wildfire spending, three new police lieutenant positions, and affordable housing funding for the Alpine Balsam site. Trade-offs included reduced funding for Spruce Pool, elimination of child watch at East Boulder Community Center, and a reduction in the photo enforcement program.

Topic4.Title: Six-year capital improvement program and long-term financial strategy
Topic4.Summary: Budget staff presented the 2027 to 2032 capital improvement program totaling $827.7 million, including utility pipeline repairs, bus priority signal improvements, wildfire prevention projects on open space, and replacement of fire stations 2 and 4. The long-term financial strategy, a comprehensive plan expected in December, and the 2026 November recreation and safety bond were also covered. The community, culture, resilience and safety tax was extended permanently by voters in 2025.

Topic5.Title: Council questions on Alpine Balsam cost history and capital project transparency
Topic5.Summary: Council Member Rob Winer raised concerns about how the Alpine Balsam project's costs and obligations have been communicated and asked how the city can be more transparent on large projects. Deputy City Manager Chris Massey said the project has stayed within council-approved budgets and that a project page and story map covering the 11-year history were published. Staff committed to considering how to tag cross-departmental projects more visibly.

Topic6.Title: Facilities reserves, 2% CRV set-aside and building maintenance bond
Topic6.Summary: Council Member Kaplan asked whether reserves are set aside for future building replacement. Staff explained the 2% capital renewal value set-aside policy and the $4.3 million added for critical facility maintenance enabled by the 3% CCRS tax. Staff said that if the November bond fails, the city would face difficult trade-offs in keeping 15 priority buildings operating.

Topic7.Title: Fund our future priorities, uniform service tiers, and trade-off framework
Topic7.Summary: Council members asked how the new service tier framework (critical, mandated, strategic priority, community enrichment) would guide future budgets and why top community priorities were not more clearly itemized. Staff described the tiering exercise and said it will be tied to work planning. Council Member Benjamin said community priorities such as wildfire, infrastructure, and public safety were spread across the budget and difficult to find.

Topic8.Title: Pools, silver sneakers discounts, and dedicated revenue restrictions
Topic8.Summary: Mayor Pro Tem Tara Winer asked whether Spruce Pool could be funded through the sugar-sweetened beverage tax or whether senior discounts could be income-based. Staff explained that voter-approved uses of those dedicated funds limit reallocation, and that Parks and Recreation is working on how best to serve older adults through a means-tested approach. The high share of restricted revenue citywide was also noted.

Topic9.Title: Internal and external auditor functions
Topic9.Summary: Council Member Winer asked how community members can request an external performance audit and how a project could be audited. Deputy City Attorney Roberto Ramirez referred to a confidential memo on the process. Staff explained the internal auditor works from an annual risk-based plan, that an audit request webpage was recently launched, and that a follow-up discussion on auditing could be scheduled.

Topic10.Title: Wildfire funding, nature-based solutions and grants
Topic10.Summary: Council Members Matt and Rob Winer proposed directing about $2 million in climate initiatives funds and additional OSMP funds toward wildfire mitigation, citing community concern about wildfire risk. Mayor Brockett and other members said they would not support that large a cut in climate funding without more analysis. Staff described nature-based wildfire work, circular economy efforts, and roughly $2.1 million in wildfire grants received.

Topic11.Title: Snow and ice removal and photo enforcement program
Topic11.Summary: Council Member Winer asked whether snow and ice removal would expand to west Boulder streets where seniors are at risk of being stuck. The director of transportation said funds allow for added equipment but not new streets this year, with a packet to come. Winer also asked why the photo enforcement van program was reduced; staff said cost outpaced revenue and officers would prioritize neighborhood complaints.

Topic12.Title: Council budget amendment process and next steps
Topic12.Summary: The deputy city attorney and budget officer explained that council members may propose substantive changes through the hotline by September 28, with an identified offset required for any balanced amendment. The first reading is October 1 and adoption October 15. Council members discussed the timing of any wildfire or other ongoing funding decisions, and the difference between the annual budget and mid-year appropriations.

Topic13.Title: Council closing comments and substantive requests
Topic13.Summary: Council members closed by reiterating concerns on Spruce Pool and the day services center, which are funded with one-time dollars, and asked how to sustain them. Council Member Adams raised concerns about evacuation, recovery and relocation funding, energy rate increases, the water supply under drought scenarios, and reduced outreach funding for community connectors. Mayor Brockett closed the meeting at 8:56 p.m. and reminded members of the September 28 hotline deadline.
